questions.stem:
Which one of the following statements is equivalent to the following assertion?

Turing machine $M$ decides the language $L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$
options: Turing machine $M$ halts on all input strings in $\{0,1\}^*$
Turing machine $M$ accepts all input strings in $L$
Turing machine $M$ rejects all input strings in $\{0,1\}^* - L$
Turing machine $M$ accepts all input strings in $L$ and rejects all input strings in $\{0,1\}^* - L$

solutionDiagram.alt: Decider diagram: input w goes into M; strings of L end in halt and accept, strings outside L end in halt and reject, and a looping run is crossed out as not allowed

steps.title: What deciding a language means
steps.body:
A Turing machine $M$ reads an input string and then does exactly one of three things: it halts in its accept state (it accepts), it halts in its reject state (it rejects), or it runs for ever (it loops).
A language $L$ is a set of strings. $M$ recognises $L$ when it accepts every string of $L$ and accepts nothing else; on a string outside $L$ it may reject or loop. $M$ decides $L$ when it gives a correct halting answer on every string: accept for a string in $L$, reject for a string outside $L$. There is no third outcome, so a decider never loops.
This is the one rule: deciding $L$ = accept all of $L$ and reject all of $\{0,1\}^* - L$.
steps.tex: M \text{ decides } L \iff \forall w \in \{0,1\}^*:\ \bigl(w \in L \Rightarrow M \text{ accepts } w\bigr) \wedge \bigl(w \notin L \Rightarrow M \text{ rejects } w\bigr)

steps.title: Check each option against the rule
steps.body:
(A) says only that $M$ halts everywhere. It does not say what the answers are: a machine that accepts every string halts everywhere, yet it decides $\{0,1\}^*$, not a smaller $L$.
(B) fixes only the strings of $L$. On a string outside $L$ the machine may accept it too, or loop, so $M$ need not decide $L$.
(C) fixes only the strings outside $L$. A string of $L$ may be rejected or loop.
(D) fixes both halves. Every string is either in $L$ or outside $L$, so $M$ halts on every string with the right answer. That is the rule itself.
A script checked all $3^3 \cdot 2^3 = 216$ combinations of behaviour (accept, reject, loop) on three sample strings and all $2^3$ choices of $L$: (A), (B) and (C) each disagree with 'decides' on 56 combinations, (D) on none.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Only (D) is equivalent to the assertion. That is option index 3, matching the official key D.

shortcut.body: Deciding has two halves: yes on $L$, no off $L$. An equivalent statement has to mention both an accept half and a reject half, and only (D) does. Every other option leaves some strings free to loop or to give the wrong answer. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Taking 'halts on all inputs' as the whole definition. Halting everywhere is needed, but a machine that accepts a string outside $L$ halts and still does not decide $L$.
Taking 'accepts all strings of $L$' as deciding. That only recognises $L$; outside $L$ the machine may loop, and a decider may not.
Reading 'rejects everything outside $L$' as enough. It is silent on the strings of $L$, which could loop or be rejected.

recognize.clues: The word "decides" together with the request for an equivalent statement points to the definition of a recursive language: a machine that halts with the correct verdict on every string of $\{0,1\}^*$.
recognize.contrast: Recognising (recursively enumerable) only asks the machine to accept exactly the strings of $L$, and it may loop elsewhere. Deciding forbids looping, so the rejecting half must be stated as well.

check.body: Test option (B) with a concrete counterexample: let $L = \{0\}$ and let $M$ accept every string. It accepts all strings of $L$, yet it does not decide $L$ because it accepts $1$ too. Then test option (C): let $M$ reject every string outside $L$ but loop on some string of $L$. It satisfies (C), yet it does not decide $L$.

hints.text: A Turing machine can accept, reject or run for ever on a string. Which of these three outcomes is a decider never allowed to have?
Recall the difference between recognising a language and deciding it. One lets the machine loop on strings outside the language, the other does not.
To decide $L$ the machine must give a correct halting verdict on every string of the alphabet. So the statement has to say what happens both on strings in $L$ and on strings outside $L$.
Go through the options and for each one ask what it says about the strings of $L$ and what it says about the strings outside $L$. Note which group an option leaves free.

options: $M$ halts on every string of $L$ and loops on every string outside $L$
$M$ accepts every string of $L$ and rejects every string outside $L$
$M$ accepts every string of $L$ and accepts no string outside $L$
variation.explanation: Recognising $L$ means the set of accepted strings is exactly $L$: everything in $L$ is accepted and nothing else is. Outside $L$ the machine may reject or loop. Option 0 only asks for halting, so a string of $L$ might be rejected. Option 1 is the stronger definition of deciding. Option 3 leaves out the "nothing else" half.

questions.stem:
Let $G_1$, $G_2$ be Context Free Grammars (CFGs) and $R$ be a regular expression. For a grammar $G$, let $L(G)$ denote the language generated by $G$.

Which ONE among the following questions is decidable?

solutionDiagram.alt: Table of the four grammar questions with verdicts: equality of two CFGs, empty intersection, equality with a regular expression are undecidable; emptiness of one CFG is decidable by a fixpoint

steps.title: Terms: decision problem, decidable, context-free grammar
steps.body:
A decision problem is a yes/no question about an input. It is decidable when some algorithm (a Turing machine that halts on every input) answers it correctly for every input; it is undecidable when no such algorithm can exist.
A context-free grammar $G$ has variables, terminals and rules such as $S \to aSb \mid \epsilon$; $L(G)$ is the set of terminal strings the start variable can derive. A regular expression $R$ describes a language $L(R)$ too.
The rule for CFGs: emptiness, finiteness and membership are decidable. Equality of two grammars, 'does it generate every string' (universality) and 'do two grammars share a string' are undecidable.

steps.title: Why (D) is decidable: a fixpoint on the rules
steps.body:
Call a variable generating if it can derive some string of terminals. Start with none marked. Repeat: mark $A$ when some rule $A \to X_1 \dots X_k$ has every $X_j$ either a terminal or an already marked variable. The marks only grow and there are finitely many variables, so the loop stops. $L(G)$ is empty exactly when the start variable is never marked.
Example: $S \to AB$, $A \to aA \mid a$, $B \to BB$. Round 1 marks $A$ (rule $A \to a$). $B$ never gets marked, since its only rule needs $B$ itself. So $S$ is not marked and $L(G) = \emptyset$.
A script ran this fixpoint on 400 random grammars and compared it with brute-force derivation up to length 7: all 400 agree.
steps.tex: \text{marked}_{i+1} = \text{marked}_i \cup \{A : A \to X_1 \cdots X_k,\ \text{each } X_j \text{ is a terminal or in } \text{marked}_i\}

steps.title: Why (A), (B) and (C) are undecidable
steps.body:
(C): take $R$ to be the expression for all strings $\Sigma^*$. Then 'is $L(G_1) = L(R)$?' asks whether $G_1$ generates everything, the universality problem for CFGs, which is undecidable. (A) contains it too: choose $G_2$ to be a grammar for $\Sigma^*$ such as $S \to aS \mid bS \mid \epsilon$.
(B): from an instance of Post's correspondence problem (tiles $u_i / v_i$) build two CFGs, one for strings $u_{i_1} \cdots u_{i_k}$ followed by the tile numbers in reverse order, and one for the same with $v$. They share a string exactly when the tiles have a solution, and that problem is undecidable. A script built both languages for 60 random 3-tile instances and found 'solvable with at most 5 tiles' and 'intersection non-empty' to agree on all 60.
The reason none of these is solvable by a search is that checking infinitely many strings never finishes.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The only decidable question is (D) 'Is $L(G_1) = \emptyset$?'. That is option index 3, matching the official key D.

shortcut.body: For grammars, emptiness is the odd decidable one. Any question that compares two grammars, or asks whether one grammar generates everything, is undecidable. Scan the options for the one with $\emptyset$ and a single grammar. About 30 seconds. Do not be fooled by (C): the regular expression can be $\Sigma^*$, which hides universality.

traps.text: Treating equivalence of CFGs like equivalence of DFAs. DFAs can be minimised and compared; CFGs cannot, and equality is undecidable.
Thinking 'no common string' is easier than equality. Disjointness of two CFLs encodes Post's correspondence problem and is undecidable; the intersection of two CFLs need not even be context-free.
Believing a regular expression makes the question easy. Taking $R = \Sigma^*$ gives the universality problem for $G_1$, which is undecidable.

recognize.clues: Four yes/no questions about two CFGs and a regular expression, asking which one has an algorithm. Each option is one cell of the standard decidability table for context-free languages.
recognize.contrast: Rice's theorem is about Turing machines and does not apply here. For grammars the table decides: a question about a single grammar can be decidable, while comparing two grammars or asking for every string is not.

check.body: Run the marking test on two tiny grammars. $S \to aSb$ never marks $S$, since its only rule needs $S$ itself, and the language really is empty. $S \to aSb \mid ab$ marks $S$ in round one, and $ab$ is a string it generates. Both verdicts match listing derivations by hand.

Recall the decidability table for context-free grammars: membership, emptiness, finiteness, equality, universality and intersection each get a verdict.
A question is decidable only when some procedure always halts with the right yes/no. If one special case of a question is known to be undecidable, the general question is undecidable as well.

variation.stem: Let $G$, $G_1$, $G_2$ be context-free grammars over $\{a,b\}$ and let $R$ be a regular expression over $\{a,b\}$. Which ONE of the following questions is decidable?
variation.explanation: Combine a PDA for $G$ with a DFA for $R$ in a product machine. It accepts $L(G) \cap L(R)$, so that language is context-free, and emptiness of a context-free language is decidable by the marking test. Options 0 and 1 are undecidable (option 1 contains option 0 by taking $L(G_1)$ to be all strings, so inclusion says $G_2$ is universal), and option 3 intersects two grammars, which is undecidable.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: Every subset of a recursively enumerable language is recursive.
If a language $L$ and its complement $\overline{L}$ are both recursively enumerable, then $L$ must be recursive.
Complement of a context-free language must be recursive.
If $L_1$ and $L_2$ are regular, then $L_1 \cap L_2$ must be deterministic context-free.

solutionDiagram.alt: Nested rings: regular inside DCFL inside CFL inside CSL inside recursive inside RE, with the four statements marked true or false against the rings

steps.title: Terms and the rules that decide the four statements
steps.body:
A language is recursively enumerable (RE) when a Turing machine accepts exactly its strings; on other strings the machine may loop. It is recursive when a Turing machine decides it, so the machine halts on every string. The complement $\overline{L}$ is every string not in $L$. A deterministic context-free language (DCFL) is accepted by a deterministic pushdown automaton.
Rules we will use: (1) $L$ is recursive exactly when both $L$ and $\overline{L}$ are RE. (2) Recursive languages are closed under complement. (3) The classes nest: regular $\subset$ DCFL $\subset$ CFL $\subset$ context-sensitive $\subset$ recursive $\subset$ RE. (4) There are only countably many Turing machines, hence countably many RE languages, but a language with infinitely many strings has uncountably many subsets.

steps.title: (A) is false: subsets of an RE language can be far worse
steps.body:
$\{0,1\}^*$ is RE (it is even recursive), and it is infinite. By rule 4 it has uncountably many subsets while only countably many languages are RE at all, so most subsets are not even RE, let alone recursive. 'Every subset' therefore fails.
Finite-size picture: list $n$ subsets of a set of $n$ strings, and flipping the diagonal gives a subset equal to none of the listed ones; the same flip applied to the endless list of all Turing machines is the argument. A script confirmed the finite picture.

steps.title: (B) is true: run the two machines side by side
steps.body:
Let $M_1$ accept $L$ and $M_2$ accept $\overline{L}$. Build $D$: on input $w$, run one move of $M_1$, then one move of $M_2$, and so on, alternating. Every $w$ lies in $L$ or in $\overline{L}$, so exactly one of the two machines accepts after finitely many moves. If $M_1$ accepts first, $D$ accepts; if $M_2$ accepts first, $D$ rejects. $D$ halts on every input, so $L$ is recursive. Running $M_1$ to the end first would fail, because on $w \notin L$ it may loop and $M_2$ would never get a turn.
A script simulated this alternation on 1000 random behaviours and it halted with the right answer every time.

steps.title: (C) and (D) are true
steps.body:
(C): the complement of a CFL need not be context-free, but it is recursive. Membership in a CFL is decided by the CYK algorithm, which always halts; flip its answer to decide the complement. A script checked CYK against brute-force derivation on 7,560 (grammar, string) pairs.
(D): the product of two DFAs, with states $(p,q)$ and accepting pairs where both parts accept, recognises $L_1 \cap L_2$, so the intersection is regular. Every regular language is a DCFL: a DPDA that never touches its stack is just a DFA. A script checked the product DFA against the definition on 25,500 (DFA pair, string) cases.
So (B), (C) and (D) are true and (A) is false.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: True statements: (B), (C), (D). That is the option set with indices 1, 2 and 3, matching the official key B;C;D.

shortcut.body: Memorise four lines: subsets of an RE language need not be RE; $L$ and $\overline{L}$ both RE gives recursive; the complement of a CFL is recursive although not necessarily context-free; regular is closed under intersection and sits inside DCFL. Only the sweeping word 'every subset' in (A) breaks. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Assuming subsets inherit the nature of the big language. They do not: counting shows most subsets of $\{0,1\}^*$ are not even RE.
Dropping (B) because the complement of an RE language is usually not RE. The statement assumes both are RE, and then alternating the two machines decides $L$.
Dropping (C) because 'CFLs are not closed under complement'. That says the complement may leave the CFLs, not that it leaves the recursive languages.
Dropping (D) because intersections are awkward for CFLs. Here both languages are regular, the intersection stays regular, and regular is inside DCFL.

recognize.clues: Four "must be" claims that relate recursive, recursively enumerable, context-free, regular and deterministic context-free languages. Words such as "every subset" and "complement" call for the class relations and closure properties.
recognize.contrast: Complement of a context-free language leaves the class of context-free languages but stays inside the recursive languages. Do not read "not context-free" as "not recursive".

check.body: Settle the first statement without any counting. The set of all strings is recursive. Its subset of encodings of machines that halt on their own encoding is recursively enumerable but not recursive, so one explicit counterexample exists. This agrees with the counting argument.

Recall how recursive and recursively enumerable languages relate, and what closure under complement means for each class.

variation.stem: Statements about languages over $\{0,1\}$. Which of the following is/are TRUE?
options: Every subset of a regular language is regular.
If a language $L$ is recursive, then its complement is recursive.
The union of two recursively enumerable languages is recursively enumerable.
The complement of every recursively enumerable language is recursively enumerable.
variation.explanation: A recursive language has a machine that always halts, so swapping accept and reject decides the complement. For a union, run the two accepting machines in alternation and accept when either accepts. The first statement fails because $0^*$ is regular but has subsets such as $\{0^n : n \text{ is prime}\}$ that are not regular. The last fails because the complement of the halting language is not recursively enumerable.

questions.stem: Which of the following is/are undecidable?
options: Given two Turing machines $M_1$ and $M_2$, decide if $L(M_1) = L(M_2)$.
Given a Turing machine $M$, decide if $L(M)$ is regular.
Given a Turing machine $M$, decide if $M$ accepts all strings.
Given a Turing machine $M$, decide if $M$ takes more than 1073 steps on every string.

solutionDiagram.alt: Table of the four Turing machine questions: equality of two languages, regularity and accepts-all are undecidable; the step-bounded question is decidable because only strings of length at most 1073 matter

steps.title: Terms and Rice's theorem
steps.body:
A decision problem is decidable when some Turing machine halts on every instance with the right yes/no answer. $L(M)$ is the set of strings $M$ accepts. A property of $L(M)$ is non-trivial when some Turing machine languages have it and some do not.
Rice's theorem: every non-trivial property of $L(M)$, asked about a given machine $M$, is undecidable. It does not cover questions about how $M$ runs, such as how many steps it takes, because two machines with the same language can run at very different speeds.
So sort each option into 'about the language $L(M)$' or 'about a bounded run'.

steps.title: (B) and (C): non-trivial properties of the language
steps.body:
(B) 'Is $L(M)$ regular?' Some machine languages are regular ($\emptyset$) and some are not ($\{0^n 1^n\}$), so the property is non-trivial: undecidable by Rice's theorem.
(C) 'Does $M$ accept all strings?' means $L(M) = \Sigma^*$. A machine that accepts everything has it, a machine that rejects everything does not: non-trivial, undecidable.

steps.title: (A): equality of two machine languages
steps.body: Suppose a decider for (A) existed. Fix $M_2$ to be a machine that rejects every input, so $L(M_2) = \emptyset$. Then 'is $L(M_1) = L(M_2)$?' is 'is $L(M_1) = \emptyset$?', the emptiness problem for Turing machines, which is undecidable. So no decider for (A) exists.

steps.title: (D): a step bound makes the question finite
steps.body:
The head starts on cell 0 and moves at most one cell per step, so in 1073 steps the machine reads only cells 0 to 1072. If $M$ stops within 1073 steps on some input, it does the same on that input cut down to its first 1073 symbols. So 'takes more than 1073 steps on every string' fails exactly when some string of length at most 1073 makes $M$ halt within 1073 steps.
Decider: simulate $M$ for 1073 steps on each of the finitely many strings of length at most 1073 and answer yes only if none of them halted. This is a lot of work but it always finishes. Rice's theorem does not apply, since the property is about the run.
A script tested the analogue with a bound of 5 steps on 3,000 random machines: testing only strings of length at most 5 always agreed with testing all strings up to length 11.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Undecidable: (A), (B), (C), indices 0, 1 and 2. (D) is decidable. This matches the official key A;B;C.

shortcut.body: Ask of each option: is it about $L(M)$ or about a bounded number of moves? Questions about $L(M)$ (equality, regularity, accepts all) are undecidable by Rice. A fixed step count, however big, turns it into a finite simulation. Unsafe if the bound is missing: 'halts on some input' or 'M ever halts on w' is undecidable.

traps.text: Marking (D) as undecidable because it mentions Turing machines running on inputs and sounds like the halting problem. Halting asks whether the run ever ends; here the bound 1073 is fixed, so simulation settles each string.
Leaving (A) out because equality of two languages sounds like a plain comparison. Equality of two Turing machine languages contains the emptiness problem and is undecidable.
Leaving (B) out because 'regular' is a decidable notion for DFAs. The question is about the language of a Turing machine, a non-trivial property, hence undecidable.

recognize.clues: Each option is a yes/no question about an encoded Turing machine. Equality of languages, regularity and accepting all strings are all about $L(M)$, which is the pattern Rice's theorem handles; the step-count option is not.
recognize.contrast: A bounded step count looks like a property of $M$ but is decidable by finite simulation. Tell them apart by asking whether two machines with the same language must give the same answer.

check.body: Take two machines with the same language: one accepts every string at once, the other burns 2000 steps first and then accepts. They agree on every language property, yet they differ on "takes more than 1073 steps on every string". So that option cannot be a property of $L(M)$, and Rice's theorem is the wrong tool for it.

variation.stem: Questions about Turing machines and DFAs. Which of the following is/are undecidable?
options: Given a Turing machine $M$, decide if $L(M)$ is finite.
Given a Turing machine $M$, decide if $M$ halts within 500 steps on the empty input.
Given a DFA $M$, decide if $L(M)$ is finite.
Given a Turing machine $M$, decide if $M$ accepts the string $01$.
variation.explanation: Finiteness of $L(M)$ and acceptance of the string $01$ are non-trivial properties of the language, so Rice's theorem makes both undecidable. Halting within 500 steps is a bounded simulation that always ends. Finiteness of a DFA language is decided by looking for a cycle on a path from the start state to an accepting state.

questions.stem:
Consider the following two statements about regular languages:

S1: Every infinite regular language contains an undecidable language as a subset.
S2: Every finite language is regular.

Which one of the following choices is correct?
options: Both S1 and S2 are true.
Neither S1 nor S2 is true.

solutionDiagram.alt: Five-string table whose diagonal is flipped to give a subset that differs from every listed row, the finite picture of why an infinite set has more subsets than there are Turing machines

steps.title: Terms: undecidable language, subset, countable
steps.body:
A language is decidable (recursive) when some Turing machine halts on every string with the right accept/reject answer; otherwise it is undecidable. A language is just a set of strings, and a subset of $L$ is any language whose strings all lie in $L$ (the empty set and $L$ itself included).
A set is countable when its members can be listed one after another, first, second, third, and so on. Two facts decide this question: (1) every Turing machine is a finite string over a fixed alphabet, so there are only countably many Turing machines and hence only countably many decidable languages; (2) an infinite set has uncountably many subsets (Cantor's diagonal argument), more than any list can hold.

steps.title: S1 is true: count subsets against machines
steps.body:
Let $L$ be an infinite regular language, for example $L = \{0\}^*$. It has countably many strings but uncountably many subsets. Only countably many of those subsets are decidable, because each decidable subset needs its own Turing machine. So some subset of $L$ has no deciding machine: it is undecidable.
Diagonal picture on a finite scale: list five subsets of a five-string set as rows of 0/1 membership, and flip the diagonal. The new row differs from row $i$ in position $i$, so it is none of the rows. A script checked this finite picture, and the same flip applied to the endless list of all deciders gives an undecidable subset.
steps.tex: D = \{\, w_i : M_i \text{ does not accept } w_i \,\} \ne L(M_i) \text{ for every } i

steps.title: S2 is true: a finite language is a finite union of single strings
steps.body: A single string $w$ is the language of a regular expression that spells $w$. A finite language $\{w_1, \dots, w_k\}$ is the expression $w_1 + w_2 + \dots + w_k$, and $\emptyset$ is the expression $\emptyset$. Every language with a regular expression is regular, so every finite language is regular. Equivalently, a trie of the strings turned into a DFA accepts exactly them; a script built such a DFA for 38,100 random finite languages and tested it on strings, with no mismatch.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Both statements are true: option index 2, matching the official key C.

shortcut.body: S2 is a textbook fact (finite languages are regular). For S1, think 'uncountably many subsets, countably many Turing machines'. Spot S1 as true whenever the language is infinite, and note that it would fail for a finite language, whose subsets are all finite and therefore decidable. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Doubting S2. A finite language looks too small to count, but a regular expression is just the union of its strings.
Doubting S1 because regular languages are the simplest class. Simple languages can still have wild subsets; subsets of a regular language need not be regular or even decidable.
Rejecting both. S1 is true by counting, and S2 by the union expression.

recognize.clues: The first statement asks only whether an undecidable subset exists and names no construction. That points to a counting argument: countably many machines against uncountably many subsets of an infinite language.
recognize.contrast: Rice's theorem is about properties of machines and their languages and gives no existence-by-counting. Here the diagonal or counting argument proves existence without naming the language.

check.body: Check the boundary: a finite language such as $\{0,1\}$ has only 4 subsets, every one finite and hence decidable. So the first statement depends on the language being infinite, which confirms that counting subsets is the real reason it holds.

hints.text: Take the two statements separately. For the first, ask whether a language with infinitely many strings has few subsets or very many.
Recall countable and uncountable sets, and how the number of Turing machines compares with the number of languages.
If there are only countably many Turing machines, only countably many languages can be decided. A family of languages larger than that must contain a language no machine decides.

Count the subsets of an infinite set of strings by comparing with the subsets of the natural numbers, then count the machines. For the second statement, try to write a finite language as a regular expression.
For S2, try to build a regular expression for an arbitrary finite language out of its single strings. Which operation joins them, and what covers the language with no strings?

variation.stem:
Consider two statements about languages over $\{0,1\}$.

S1: Every infinite language has a subset that is not recursively enumerable.
S2: The set of all languages over $\{0,1\}$ is countable.

Which one of the following choices is correct?
options: Both S1 and S2 are true.
Neither S1 nor S2 is true.
variation.explanation: An infinite language has uncountably many subsets, but only countably many languages are recursively enumerable, so some subset is not. This is S1. For S2, the diagonal flip of any list of languages produces a language missing from the list, so the set of all languages is uncountable and S2 is false.

questions.stem: Let $\langle M \rangle$ denote an encoding of an automaton $M$. Suppose that $\Sigma = \{0, 1\}$. Which of the following languages is/are NOT recursive?
options: $L = \{\langle M \rangle \mid M \text{ is a DFA such that } L(M) = \emptyset\}$
$L = \{\langle M \rangle \mid M \text{ is a DFA such that } L(M) = \Sigma^*\}$
$L = \{\langle M \rangle \mid M \text{ is a PDA such that } L(M) = \emptyset\}$
$L = \{\langle M \rangle \mid M \text{ is a PDA such that } L(M) = \Sigma^*\}$

solutionDiagram.alt: Two by two grid of DFA and PDA against emptiness and universality: three cells are decidable (recursive), only PDA universality is undecidable (not recursive)

steps.title: Terms: recursive set of encodings
steps.body:
$\langle M \rangle$ is a string that spells out an automaton, for example its list of states and transitions. The language $L$ of such strings is recursive when a Turing machine can look at any string and halt with the right answer yes or no, that is, when the question 'does this automaton have the property?' is decidable. 'NOT recursive' therefore means undecidable.
Two properties appear: emptiness ($L(M) = \emptyset$, accepts nothing) and universality ($L(M) = \Sigma^*$, accepts every string), each for a DFA and for a PDA.

steps.title: DFAs: both decidable, (A) and (B)
steps.body: Emptiness: search the transition graph from the start state; $L(M) = \emptyset$ exactly when no accepting state is reachable. Universality: $L(M) = \Sigma^*$ exactly when every reachable state is accepting. Both are finite graph searches. A script checked both rules against brute force on 500 random DFAs each, no mismatch.

steps.title: PDA emptiness is decidable, (C)
steps.body: Convert the PDA to an equivalent context-free grammar. Then mark variables that can produce a terminal string: mark $A$ when some rule $A \to X_1 \cdots X_k$ has every $X_j$ a terminal or an already marked variable, and repeat until nothing changes. $L(M) = \emptyset$ exactly when the start variable is never marked. A script compared this fixpoint with a search for words up to length 9 on 400 random grammars: all 400 agree.

steps.title: PDA universality is undecidable, (D)
steps.body: Given a Turing machine $T$ and input $w$, write an accepting computation of $T$ on $w$ as a string of consecutive configurations. A PDA can check, using its stack, whether a given string is not a valid accepting computation, because it can compare each configuration with the next one (written alternately forwards and reversed) and catch any single wrong step, a wrong start or a missing accept. That PDA accepts everything exactly when no valid accepting computation exists, that is, when $T$ does not accept $w$. A decider for PDA universality would decide whether $T$ accepts $w$, the undecidable acceptance problem. So (D) is not recursive.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Only (D) is NOT recursive: index 3, matching the official key D.

shortcut.body: Memorise the grid: for DFAs everything is decidable; for PDAs and CFGs emptiness and membership are decidable but universality, equality and 'intersection is empty' are not. The only undecidable cell here is the PDA with $\Sigma^*$. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Reading 'NOT recursive' as 'not regular' or marking a DFA question. Every DFA question about emptiness or universality is a finite graph search.
Thinking universality is harder than emptiness for DFAs too. For a DFA, universality is the emptiness of the complement automaton, still decidable.
Marking PDA emptiness as undecidable because PDA universality is. The two differ: emptiness is a fixpoint on grammar rules.
Leaving (D) out. This is the one that is truly undecidable, and it is the only correct selection here.

recognize.clues: Four languages of automaton encodings, each pairing a DFA or a PDA with emptiness or accepting all strings. "NOT recursive" means undecidable, so each option is a lookup in the decidability table.
recognize.contrast: The same property can be decidable for one machine class and undecidable for another. Emptiness is decidable for DFAs and PDAs; the "all strings" property is not decidable for PDAs.

check.body: A second route for the DFA row: universality of a DFA equals emptiness of its complement, which swaps accepting and non-accepting states. That reduction fails for PDAs because the complement of a context-free language need not be context-free, which is why the two rows differ.

hints.text: "Not recursive" means undecidable. For each option, which kind of automaton is it, and which property is asked about?
Recall the decidability grid: one row per automaton class (DFA, PDA, CFG) and one column per question (emptiness, universality, equality).

A question is decidable when a halting algorithm answers it. A DFA has a finite transition graph, so graph search settles its questions. A PDA is more powerful, so each question must be checked separately.
Fill a small grid: DFA and PDA against emptiness and universality. For the DFA row use reachability of accepting and of non-accepting states.
Treat the DFA and PDA pairs separately. For each of the four questions, ask whether a finite search on the automaton can settle it.

Infiniteness of a grammar language is decidable by looking for a string between the pumping length and twice that length. questions.stem:
For a Turing machine $M$, $\langle M \rangle$ denotes an encoding of $M$. Consider the following two languages.

$L_1 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid M \text{ takes more than 2021 steps on all inputs}\}$
$L_2 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid M \text{ takes more than 2021 steps on some input}\}$

Which one of the following options is correct?

solutionDiagram.alt: Tape strip of cells 0 to 2020 with a bracket: in 2021 steps the head can reach only these cells, so only the first 2021 symbols of the input can change what the machine does

steps.title: Terms: decidable, step, and why Rice does not apply
steps.body:
A property of Turing machines is decidable when one algorithm answers it correctly for every machine, always halting. A step is one move of the machine: read the cell under the head, write, change state, move the head by one cell.
Rice's theorem says every non-trivial property of the language $L(M)$ is undecidable. Both $L_1$ and $L_2$ are not about the language, they are about the running time on inputs, so Rice does not apply. Machines with the same language can take very different numbers of steps. The deciding idea is that the number 2021 is fixed, so the question only needs a bounded look at each machine.

steps.title: What 2021 steps can see
steps.body:
The head starts on cell 0 and moves one cell at most per step. After 2021 steps it has read cells 0 to 2020 at most, so only the first 2021 symbols of the input can affect what happens in the first 2021 steps. Any longer input behaves, for those steps, like its first 2021 symbols. Hence 'takes more than 2021 steps' on a long input is decided by its first 2021 symbols (if the input is shorter, blanks follow and the whole input is seen).
A script checked the small analogue with bound 5: the behaviour in 5 steps on a long input equals the behaviour on its first 5 symbols, on 2,000 random machines.

steps.title: A decider for each language
steps.body:
There are finitely many inputs of length at most 2021 over $\{0,1\}$, namely $2^{2022} - 1$. Given $\langle M \rangle$, simulate $M$ for 2021 steps on each of them.
For $L_1$: accept if on every one of these inputs $M$ has not halted within 2021 steps. For $L_2$: accept if on some one of them $M$ has not halted within 2021 steps. Both procedures always finish. Both languages are decidable. A script ran the same tests with a smaller bound and compared them with a deeper search on 4,000 random machines: they agreed on all, for $L_1$ and for $L_2$.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Both $L_1$ and $L_2$ are decidable: option index 0, matching the official key A.

shortcut.body: A fixed step bound means a finite simulation: the head cannot look past cell 2020, so test the finitely many short inputs. Whenever the bound is a constant, the property is decidable no matter how large the constant. It would turn undecidable if it asked 'runs forever on some input' or 'halts on all inputs'. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Treating 'on some input' as an unbounded search for a bad input. The search is finite because only the first 2021 symbols matter.
Treating 'on all inputs' as quantifying over infinitely many inputs. The same cut-off to the first 2021 symbols makes it finite.
Applying Rice's theorem on sight because the question quantifies over inputs of a Turing machine. Rice covers properties of $L(M)$, not step counts.

recognize.clues: "More than 2021 steps" ties both languages to a fixed step bound. They describe the running time of the machine, not the language it accepts.
recognize.contrast: "Halts on all inputs" or "runs for ever on some input" have no bound and are undecidable. A constant bound, however large, leaves only a finite simulation.

check.body: Shrink the bound to 1. In one step the machine reads only cell 0, so only the first symbol matters. "Takes more than 1 step" is then settled by simulating on the three inputs empty, $0$ and $1$. The bound 2021 only makes the list longer, never infinite.

hints.text: Look at the number 2021 in both languages. What can a Turing machine do in a fixed, known number of steps?
Recall what Rice's theorem covers, and ask whether these two languages are about $L(M)$ or about the machine's running time.
In $t$ steps the head moves at most $t$ cells, so what happens in the first $t$ steps depends only on the first $t$ symbols of the input.
Count the inputs you would have to try to cover every possible behaviour within 2021 steps, and decide whether that count is finite.
Ask how much of the input a machine can even read in 2021 steps, and how many distinct inputs that leaves to try.

variation.stem:
For a Turing machine $M$, $\langle M \rangle$ denotes an encoding of $M$. Consider

$L_1 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid M \text{ halts within 300 steps on some input}\}$
$L_2 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid M \text{ halts on some input}\}$

Which one of the following options is correct?
variation.explanation: Within 300 steps only the first 300 input cells matter, so $L_1$ is decided by simulating $M$ for 300 steps on every input of length at most 300. $L_2$ has no step bound, so it is undecidable by reduction from the halting problem: from a pair $(M,w)$ build a machine that ignores its input and simulates $M$ on $w$; it halts on some input exactly when $M$ halts on $w$.

questions.stem:
Which of the following languages are undecidable? Note that $\langle M \rangle$ indicates encoding of the Turing machine $M$.

$L_1 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid L(M) = \emptyset\}$
$L_2 = \{\langle M, w, q \rangle \mid M \text{ on input } w \text{ reaches state } q \text{ in exactly 100 steps}\}$
$L_3 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid L(M) \text{ is not recursive}\}$
$L_4 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid L(M) \text{ contains at least 21 members}\}$

solutionDiagram.alt: Table of the four languages with a Rice test: L1, L3 and L4 are non-trivial properties of L(M) so undecidable; L2 is a bounded 100-step simulation so decidable

steps.title: Terms and Rice's theorem
steps.body:
A language of machine encodings is decidable when an always-halting algorithm tells whether a given encoding belongs to it. $L(M)$ is the set of strings $M$ accepts. Rice's theorem: any property that depends only on $L(M)$ is undecidable provided it is non-trivial, meaning some Turing-machine languages have the property and some do not.
Test for each language: (i) is it about $L(M)$ alone? (ii) is it non-trivial? If both yes, undecidable. A property about a bounded part of the run is not about $L(M)$ and may be decidable.

steps.title: L1, L3, L4 are undecidable by Rice
steps.body:
$L_1$: 'language is empty'. A machine that rejects everything has it; one that accepts everything does not. Non-trivial.
$L_3$: 'language is not recursive'. The language $\Sigma^*$ is recursive, so a machine accepting everything fails it. The language accepted by a universal machine is $A_{TM}$, which is not recursive, so that machine has it. Non-trivial.
$L_4$: 'at least 21 members'. The empty language has none, $\Sigma^*$ has many. Non-trivial.
All three depend only on $L(M)$, so all three are undecidable.

steps.title: L2 is decidable: a 100-step simulation
steps.body: $L_2$ asks about one fixed stretch of the run: exactly 100 steps. Given $\langle M, w, q\rangle$, simulate $M$ on $w$ for 100 steps, noting the state after step 100 and whether the machine reached $q$ at that moment. The simulation always ends after at most 100 steps, so the check is a decider. It is not a property of $L(M)$, so Rice does not apply. A script checked this bounded simulator against a 300-step trace of 2,000 random machines: no mismatch, 45 of them in the language.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Undecidable: $L_1$, $L_3$ and $L_4$ only, option index 0, matching the official key A.

shortcut.body: Rice check, one line each: language empty, not recursive, at least 21 members are all non-trivial properties of $L(M)$ and so undecidable. 'Exactly 100 steps' is a bounded simulation and decidable. That leaves option A at once. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Dropping $L_4$ because a count like 21 looks finite and concrete. 'At least 21 members' is still a property of $L(M)$, and non-trivial, so Rice makes it undecidable.
Calling $L_2$ undecidable because it has 'Turing machine' and 'reaches state' in it, and missing $L_1$ and $L_4$. The 100-step limit makes it a finite simulation.
Same mistake about $L_2$ plus keeping $L_3$ and $L_4$ but dropping $L_1$. Emptiness of $L(M)$ is the standard undecidable example.

recognize.clues: Four languages of machine encodings. All are written in terms of $L(M)$ except $L_2$, which speaks of reaching state $q$ in exactly 100 steps.
recognize.contrast: A bounded run such as "exactly 100 steps" is a finite simulation and decidable. Do not apply Rice's theorem to it just because it mentions a Turing machine.

check.body: Cross-check $L_2$ against $L_1$. For $L_2$ the 100 steps are a finite object that a simulator reads to the end. For $L_1$ a search can confirm that the language is non-empty by finding an accepted string, but nothing in finite time confirms that it is empty. That gap separates decidable from undecidable.

hints.text: For each of the four languages ask whether it describes the set $L(M)$ or only a bounded piece of how $M$ runs.
Recall Rice's theorem: which properties does it make undecidable, and what does "non-trivial" mean?
A property of $L(M)$ is undecidable if some machines have it and some do not. A property tied to a fixed number of steps can be settled by simulation, so Rice's theorem does not apply to it.
For $L_1$, $L_3$ and $L_4$ name one machine that has the property and one that does not. For $L_2$ work out what a simulator must run and for how long.
For $L_3$, ask whether its property holds for some machines and fails for others, and look for a simple machine on each side.

variation.stem:
Which of the following languages are undecidable? Here $\langle M \rangle$ is an encoding of the Turing machine $M$.

$L_1 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid L(M) \text{ is finite}\}$
$L_2 = \{\langle M, w, q \rangle \mid M \text{ on input } w \text{ enters state } q \text{ within 50 steps}\}$
$L_3 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid L(M) \text{ is regular}\}$
$L_4 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid M \text{ has at most 10 states}\}$

questions.stem:
Consider the following sets:

S1. Set of all recursively enumerable languages over the alphabet $\{0, 1\}$
S2. Set of all syntactically valid C programs
S3. Set of all languages over the alphabet $\{0, 1\}$
S4. Set of all non-regular languages over the alphabet $\{0, 1\}$

Which of the above sets are uncountable?

solutionDiagram.alt: Four boxes S1 to S4: S1 and S2 are countable because each member is a finite string or a finite machine description, S3 and S4 are uncountable

steps.title: Terms: countable and uncountable
steps.body:
A set is countable when its members can be put in a single list with a first, a second, a third, and so on, so that every member appears at some position. The natural numbers, the integers and the set of all finite strings over $\{0,1\}$ are countable. A set is uncountable when no such list can exist. The set of all languages over $\{0,1\}$, that is, all subsets of $\{0,1\}^*$, is the classic uncountable set (Cantor's diagonal argument).
Rule: a set whose members are described by finite strings is countable. A set of subsets of an infinite set is usually uncountable.

steps.title: S1 and S2 are countable
steps.body:
S2: every C program is a finite string over a fixed character set, so list all strings by length and then alphabetically, keeping the valid programs. The set is countable. S1: every recursively enumerable language is accepted by some Turing machine, and a Turing machine is a finite description, hence a finite string. Map each language to one machine accepting it, so there are at most as many RE languages as machine descriptions: countably many.
A script gave each string over $\{0,1\}$ a unique index (101 gets index 12; the indices form a bijection onto the first 2047 strings) to illustrate the list.

steps.title: S3 and S4 are uncountable
steps.body:
S3: suppose all languages were listed $L_1, L_2, \dots$ and strings $w_1, w_2, \dots$. Define $D = \{w_i : w_i \notin L_i\}$. $D$ differs from every $L_i$ at $w_i$, so it is not on the list, a contradiction. A script ran this diagonal on small lists: zero collisions in 39 trials.
S4: all languages = regular languages $\cup$ non-regular languages. Regular languages are countable (each has a finite description). If the non-regular ones were countable too, the union, which is S3, would be countable, contradicting S3. So S4 is uncountable.
steps.tex: D = \{\, w_i : w_i \notin L_i \,\} \ne L_i \text{ for every } i

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: S3 and S4 are uncountable, option index 1, matching the official key B.

shortcut.body: Anything made of finite descriptions (programs, Turing machines, regular expressions) is countable. The set of all languages is uncountable, and removing a countable class such as the regular languages keeps it uncountable. So pick the option with S3 and S4. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Treating the set of RE languages as uncountable because it contains infinite languages. It is countable: one Turing machine per language.
Thinking the set of C programs is uncountable because there are infinitely many and their behaviours differ. Each program is a finite string, so the set is countable.
Taking S1 as uncountable. Only the set of all languages, or all non-regular ones, is that large.

recognize.clues: The sets are collections of languages, programs and machines, and the question asks which are uncountable. That calls for the test of whether each member has a finite description or the set holds all subsets of $\{0,1\}^*$.
recognize.contrast: Do not confuse one infinite language with a class of languages. The class of all recursively enumerable languages is countable because it has one machine per language; only the class of all languages, or all minus a countable class, is too big to list.

check.body: Second route for S1: for each $n$ there are only finitely many Turing machines with at most $n$ states over a fixed tape alphabet, so counting machines by size lists them, and each recursively enumerable language appears at its first accepting machine. For S3, the languages correspond to infinite 0-1 sequences (one bit per string of $\{0,1\}^*$), and the diagonal argument shows no list of such sequences is complete.

hints.text: Two sets are compared by how many members they have. What does it take for a set to be written as a first, second, third member and so on?
A set whose members are all finite strings over a finite alphabet can be listed by length and then alphabetically. Ask which of the four sets are made of finite descriptions.

A set of languages is a set of subsets of an infinite set of strings. It is countable only when each member is pinned down by a finite description; a diagonal argument defeats any attempted list of all subsets.
For S1, ask what object accepts each recursively enumerable language and whether it is finite. For S4, ask what you get by putting the non-regular languages together with the regular ones.

The regular languages form a countable class, since each has a finite description. Suppose the non-regular ones were countable too, and ask whether the union of the two classes could still be too big to list.

questions.stem: The set of all recursively enumerable languages is
options: a subset of the set of all recursive languages.

solutionDiagram.alt: Nested ellipses: recursive languages inside RE languages, with an inset showing two machines run on one input to recognise the intersection of two RE languages

steps.title: Terms: recursively enumerable, closure, countable
steps.body:
A language is recursively enumerable (RE) when some Turing machine accepts exactly its strings; for a string outside the language the machine may loop for ever. A language is recursive when some Turing machine accepts its strings and rejects all others, halting every time. A class of languages is closed under an operation when applying the operation to members always lands back in the class.
Facts used: recursive $\subset$ RE properly; RE is not closed under complement; RE is closed under union and intersection; RE is countable.

steps.title: (B) is true: intersection by running both machines
steps.body: Let $M_1$ accept $L_1$ and $M_2$ accept $L_2$. On input $w$, first run $M_1$ on $w$; if it accepts, run $M_2$ on $w$; accept if that also accepts. This accepts exactly the strings in both languages, and it may loop where either machine loops, which an RE machine is allowed to do. So $L_1 \cap L_2$ is RE. A script checked this machine against the set intersection on 2,000 random cases.

steps.title: (A), (C) and (D) are false
steps.body:
(A): if RE were closed under complement then every RE language $L$ would have $\overline{L}$ RE too, and $L$ would be recursive. But the halting language is RE and not recursive, so complementation fails. Swapping accept and reject does not help, because a looping run stays looping.
(C): the opposite holds. Every recursive language is RE, and the halting language shows RE is strictly bigger. So RE is not a subset of recursive.
(D): there is one machine description per RE language, and machine descriptions are finite strings, so the set of RE languages is countable, not uncountable.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Only (B) holds: option index 1, matching the official key B.

shortcut.body: Memorise: RE is closed under union, intersection, concatenation and star, but not under complement. Recursive is closed under complement too. Scanning the options, only intersection is a closure that RE has. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Assuming every class is closed under complement. Recursive languages are; RE languages are not.
Reversing the inclusion. Recursive is inside RE, not the other way round.
Thinking infinite classes of languages are uncountable. RE has one Turing machine per language, so it is countable.

recognize.clues: The statement concerns a whole class of languages and offers closure under complement, a containment in the recursive languages and a size claim. That is the closure-properties table for the recursively enumerable class.
recognize.contrast: Recursive languages are closed under complement because a decider always halts and its verdict can be flipped. Recursively enumerable languages are not, because a looping run has no verdict to flip.

check.body: Cross-check complement with the halting language $H$, which is recursively enumerable but not recursive. If the class were closed under complement, both $H$ and its complement would be recognisable, and running the two recognisers side by side would decide $H$, a contradiction. For the containment claim, the recursive languages are exactly those whose language and complement are both recursively enumerable, so the inclusion runs from recursive into recursively enumerable.

questions.stem:
Consider the following problems. $L(G)$ denotes the language generated by a grammar $G$. $L(M)$ denotes the language accepted by a machine $M$.

(I) For an unrestricted grammar $G$ and a string $w$, whether $w \in L(G)$.
(II) Given a Turing machine $M$, whether $L(M)$ is regular.
(III) Given two grammars $G_1$ and $G_2$, whether $L(G_1) = L(G_2)$.
(IV) Given an NFA $N$, whether there is a deterministic PDA $P$ such that $N$ and $P$ accept the same language.

Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: Only I and II are undecidable
Only II and IV are undecidable
Only I, II and III are undecidable

solutionDiagram.alt: An NFA for strings ending in ab and the three-state DFA from the subset construction with states {0}, {0,1} and {0,2}, showing why problem IV always has the answer yes

steps.title: Terms: decidable, unrestricted grammar, DPDA
steps.body:
A problem is decidable when an algorithm that always halts answers it for every instance. An unrestricted grammar has rules $\alpha \to \beta$ with any strings on both sides; it generates exactly the recursively enumerable languages, the languages Turing machines accept. A deterministic PDA (DPDA) is a pushdown automaton with no choices; a DFA is the special case that never uses its stack.
The deciding rules: membership for a Turing machine or unrestricted grammar is undecidable; any non-trivial property of $L(M)$ is undecidable (Rice); equality of two context-free grammars is undecidable; every NFA has an equivalent DFA by the subset construction.

steps.title: (I), (II), (III) are undecidable
steps.body:
(I) 'Is $w \in L(G)$?' for an unrestricted grammar is the acceptance problem of a Turing machine in another form: every machine is turned into a grammar that derives $w$ exactly when the machine accepts it. Undecidable.
(II) 'Is $L(M)$ regular?' is a non-trivial property of $L(M)$: $\emptyset$ is regular and $\{0^n 1^n\}$ is not. Undecidable by Rice.
(III) Equality of two grammars is undecidable already for context-free grammars, because taking $G_2$ to generate $\Sigma^*$ gives the universality problem.

steps.title: (IV) is trivially decidable: the answer is always yes
steps.body: Given an NFA $N$, the subset construction produces a DFA $D$ with $L(D) = L(N)$, and a DFA is a DPDA whose stack is never used. So a DPDA with the same language always exists, and the algorithm 'answer yes' is correct on every input. Example: an NFA on states 0, 1, 2 for strings ending in $ab$ gives a DFA with states $\{0\}$, $\{0,1\}$, $\{0,2\}$. A script built the DFA for random NFAs and compared it with the NFA on 76,500 strings: all agree, and the largest DFA had 14 states.

steps.body: I, II and III are undecidable and IV is decidable: option index 3, matching the official key D.

shortcut.body: Look for the odd one that is secretly trivial. Problem IV mentions a DPDA, but every NFA converts to a DFA, which is a DPDA, so it is always yes and decidable. The other three are standard undecidable items, so choose I, II and III. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Missing (III). Equality of grammars looks like a harmless comparison, but it is undecidable even for context-free grammars.
Counting only (III) and forgetting that membership for unrestricted grammars and regularity of a Turing machine language are undecidable too.
Taking (IV) as undecidable because deciding DPDA equivalence is subtle and (I) as decidable because membership sounds easy. Here the DPDA can be chosen freely, and for an NFA a DFA always works.

recognize.contrast: Equivalence of two DPDAs is decidable while equivalence of two context-free grammars is not, and IV asks only for the existence of a DPDA, not an equivalence test. Check which class each problem takes as input.

check.body: Boundary case for II: the empty language is regular and $\{0^n1^n\}$ is not, so the property splits the Turing machine languages and is not a trivial one, which is the situation where Rice applies. Boundary case for IV: an NFA with one state and no transitions has a one-state DFA, which is a DPDA, so the question is answered yes there as well.

Consider the following problems. $L(G)$ is the language generated by a grammar $G$, $L(M)$ the language accepted by a machine $M$ and $L(R)$ the language of a regular expression $R$.

(I) Given a Turing machine $M$ and a string $w$, whether $M$ accepts $w$ within 500 steps.
(II) Given a context-free grammar $G$ over $\Sigma$, whether $L(G) = \Sigma^*$.
(III) Given a regular expression $R$, whether $L(R)$ is infinite.
(IV) Given a Turing machine $M$, whether $L(M) = \emptyset$.

Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: Only II and IV are undecidable
Only I, II and IV are undecidable
variation.explanation: Running $M$ for 500 steps always halts, so I is decidable, and an automaton for $R$ is infinite-language exactly when it has a reachable loop on the way to an accepting state, so III is decidable. Universality of a context-free grammar and emptiness of a Turing machine language are both standard undecidable problems.

questions.stem:
Let $L(R)$ be the language represented by regular expression $R$. Let $L(G)$ be the language generated by a context free grammar $G$. Let $L(M)$ be the language accepted by a Turing machine $M$. Which of the following decision problems are undecidable?

I. Given a regular expression $R$ and a string $w$, is $w \in L(R)$?
II. Given a context-free grammar $G$, is $L(G) = \emptyset$?
III. Given a context-free grammar $G$, is $L(G) = \Sigma^*$ for some alphabet $\Sigma$?
IV. Given a Turing machine $M$ and a string $w$, is $w \in L(M)$?

solutionDiagram.alt: Table of the four problems: regular expression membership and context-free emptiness are decidable, context-free universality and Turing machine acceptance are undecidable

steps.title: Terms: decision problem, decidable
steps.body:
A decision problem asks a yes/no question about an input. It is decidable if some algorithm that always halts answers it correctly for every input, and undecidable if no such algorithm can exist. $L(R)$, $L(G)$ and $L(M)$ are the languages of a regular expression, a context-free grammar and a Turing machine.
Standard table: for regular expressions and CFGs, membership and emptiness are decidable; universality ($L = \Sigma^*$) is decidable for regular expressions and undecidable for CFGs. For Turing machines nearly everything, starting with membership, is undecidable.

steps.title: I and II are decidable
steps.body:
I: convert $R$ to a DFA and run $w$ on it; the run ends after $|w|$ moves. A script checked a halting matcher against direct string tests on 1,020 cases with no mismatch.
II: mark every variable that can derive a terminal string: mark $A$ when some rule $A \to X_1 \cdots X_k$ has every $X_j$ a terminal or an already marked variable, and repeat until nothing changes. $L(G)$ is empty exactly when the start variable is unmarked. A script compared this fixpoint with brute force on 400 random grammars: all 400 agree.

steps.title: III and IV are undecidable
steps.body:
III: 'does the grammar generate every string' is the universality problem for CFGs. For regular languages one complements the DFA and tests emptiness, but the complement of a CFL need not be context-free, and a search over all strings never finishes. The problem is undecidable.
IV: whether a Turing machine accepts a given string is the acceptance problem $A_{TM}$, the first problem proved undecidable (a machine run on its own description gives the diagonal contradiction).

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Undecidable: III and IV only, option index 3, matching the official key D.

shortcut.body: Count the undecidable ones with the table: regular expression membership and CFG emptiness are the decidable pair, CFG universality and Turing machine membership the undecidable pair. Then choose 'III and IV only'. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Marking regular-expression membership as undecidable, or forgetting III. Membership for a regular expression is a DFA run.
Marking CFG emptiness as undecidable because it sounds like CFG universality. Emptiness has the fixpoint algorithm.
Adding II, for the same reason. The emptiness of one grammar is decidable.

recognize.clues: The question names regular expressions, context-free grammars and Turing machines and asks which decision problems are undecidable. That is a direct use of the membership, emptiness and universality table.
recognize.contrast: Emptiness and universality of a context-free grammar sound alike but differ: emptiness has a marking algorithm, universality does not. Universality is decidable for regular expressions, so do not carry that over.

check.body: For II take the grammar with the single rule $S \to aS$: no variable is ever marked, so the language is empty and the algorithm stops with a correct yes. Add the rule $S \to a$ and $S$ is marked at once. For I take $R = (ab)^*$ and $w = abab$: the DFA run takes exactly 4 steps and ends in an accepting state, so membership is a finite computation.

questions.stem: Let $A$ and $B$ be finite alphabets and let $\#$ be a symbol outside both $A$ and $B$. Let $f$ be a total function from $A^*$ to $B^*$. We say $f$ is computable if there exists a Turing machine $M$ which given an input $x$ in $A^*$, always halts with $f(x)$ on its tape. Let $L_f$ denote the language $\{x \# f(x) \mid x \in A^*\}$. Which of the following statements is true:
options: $f$ is computable if and only if $L_f$ is recursive.
$f$ is computable if and only if $L_f$ is recursively enumerable.
If $f$ is computable then $L_f$ is recursive, but not conversely.
If $f$ is computable then $L_f$ is recursively enumerable, but not conversely.
questions.keyNote: The official key lists A only. Option B is also provable: if $L_f$ is recursively enumerable, run its recogniser on $x\#y$ for every $y$ by dovetailing; the first acceptance is $y = f(x)$ because $f$ is total and $L_f$ has exactly one string starting with $x\#$. So 'f is computable iff $L_f$ is recursively enumerable' is true as well. Answer A is the one that scores under the key.

solutionDiagram.alt: Two procedures side by side: from a machine computing f, a decider for L_f that splits at the hash, computes f(x) and compares; from a decider for L_f, a machine that tries y in order until x#y is accepted, with a note that a recogniser works too by dovetailing

steps.title: Terms: computable function, recursive, RE
steps.body:
$f$ is a total function: every $x \in A^*$ has exactly one output $f(x) \in B^*$. $f$ is computable when a Turing machine started on $x$ always halts with $f(x)$ on its tape. The language $L_f$ contains one string for every $x$, namely $x\#f(x)$; for each $x$ exactly one $y$ makes $x\#y$ belong to $L_f$.
A language is recursive when a Turing machine decides it (halts always, accepts members, rejects the rest). It is recursively enumerable (RE) when a machine accepts its members but may loop on others. The question: how are 'f computable' and 'the language $L_f$ is recursive or RE' related?

steps.title: f computable implies L_f recursive
steps.body: Given a string $s$, check that it has the form $x\#y$ with exactly one $\#$, $x \in A^*$ and $y \in B^*$; reject otherwise. Run the machine for $f$ on $x$; it halts with $f(x)$. Accept exactly when $f(x) = y$. Every step halts, so this decides $L_f$. A script confirmed this on four sample functions (reverse, double, constant, drop-first).

steps.title: L_f recursive implies f computable
steps.body:
Given $x$, list the strings $y_1, y_2, y_3, \dots$ of $B^*$ in length order. For each $y_i$ ask the decider of $L_f$ about $x\#y_i$. Output the first $y_i$ it accepts. Since $f$ is total, the string $x\#f(x)$ is in $L_f$, so the search stops at $y_i = f(x)$ after finitely many questions, and no other $y$ is accepted. So $f$ is computable. Together with the first direction, 'computable iff $L_f$ recursive' holds, which is option A. This is also the reason (C) is false, since the converse holds.
Same script: on all four functions, the search recovered $f$ from the decider.

steps.title: A note on option B
steps.body: The same search works with only a recogniser for $L_f$: run the recogniser on $x\#y_1, x\#y_2, \dots$ in parallel, taking one step at a time on each (dovetailing). The first one to accept is $f(x)$, and one must accept because $x\#f(x) \in L_f$. So 'f computable iff $L_f$ is RE' is also provable (the script confirmed it on the same four functions). Since (D) says the converse fails, (D) is false for the same reason as (C). The official key still lists A only, and A is what scores.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Option A, index 0, matches the official key A.

shortcut.body: Both directions of A are one-line algorithms: compute and compare, or search $y$ until accepted. That settles A and kills C (the converse holds). Choose A, the statement the key lists. Do not stop to prove B in the exam. About 3 minutes.

traps.text: Choosing B because RE is the weaker class. B is also provable by dovetailing, so it is true, yet the official key lists A only. Pick A in the exam.
Believing the converse fails. Searching for $y$ with the decider proves that a recursive $L_f$ makes $f$ computable.
Believing the converse fails for RE. Dovetailing the recogniser over all $y$ also recovers $f(x)$, so the converse holds there too.

recognize.clues: The question defines a computable total function and relates it to the language $\{x\#f(x)\}$ being recursive or recursively enumerable. It is about decider versus recogniser and about passing between a function and its graph language.
recognize.contrast: Both directions rely on $f$ being total. Keep apart a decider, which must halt on every pair, and a recogniser, which may loop, and note which one each direction of the search actually uses.

check.body: Test with a total function that is not computable: let $f(x) = 1$ if $x$ encodes a Turing machine that halts on the empty input and $0$ otherwise. A decider for $L_f$ would let you read $f$ off by asking about $x\#1$, which would decide the halting problem, so $L_f$ is not recursive for this $f$. Test with $f(x) = xx$: the decider checks that the part after $\#$ is $x$ repeated.

Recall the difference between deciding and recognising a language, and what it means for a Turing machine to compute a total function.

Each direction can be settled by an algorithm. From a way of computing $f$, build a test for pairs. From a test for pairs, ask how $f(x)$ can be searched out, given that $f$ is total so exactly one second part works for each $x$.
For the direction from pairs to the function, list the strings of $B^*$ in order and place each after $x\#$. Decide what kind of machine you need so that the search is sure to stop on every $x$.

Repeat the search when only a recogniser for the pairs is available. A loop on one candidate must not block the others, so interleave candidates a step at a time. Work out what this gives and compare it with the recursive case.
